passage:
I'm Lata, and I live next to Chandrika's room, so I heard most of it.

On Monday at dinner, Chandrika was the centre of the table, telling everyone that Amandeep had been failing calculus and hiding it from home. People laughed a little, then went quiet when one of Amandeep's friends looked over. Chandrika's laugh trailed off.

Later that night I heard her at Amandeep's door. No excuses, as far as I could tell. "I told them your thing. I wanted them to listen to me. It was wrong, and I'm sorry." Amandeep said, "I need some space right now." Chandrika said, "Okay. I understand," and went back to her room.

I can't say what either of them felt. I only know Chandrika skipped breakfast for two days.

qa.q: What did Chandrika tell the table about Amandeep?
qa.a: That Amandeep had been failing calculus and hiding it from home.

qa.q: What might Chandrika's trailing laugh suggest, and why can't Lata be sure?
qa.a: It might suggest Chandrika felt caught or uneasy when Amandeep's friend looked over. Lata only saw behaviour and cannot know the inner state for sure.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do that a wise person would?
qa.a: Owned it quickly, apologised without excuses and accepted Amandeep's request for space.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt hearing this at the door?
qa.a: Probably exposed and hurt, and asking for space suggests trust will need time to come back, if it does.

grounding: Chandrika shared a friend's confidence for attention, then owned it and apologised without excuses, seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Saturday: At the hostel terrace party, the group was laughing about crushes, and Nitin, wanting a bigger laugh, blurted out that Varun still wrote letters to his ex that he never sent. Everyone roared. Varun, by the water tank, went very still and left.
Sunday: Nitin woke up sick with it. His first draft of a message said, "Bro, chill, it was just a joke, nobody cares." He deleted it and knocked on Varun's door instead. "I told them something you trusted me with, because I wanted the laugh. That was wrong. No excuse. I'm sorry." Varun said, "Okay," and closed the door.
The next Friday: Varun still sat at the other end of the mess table. Nitin didn't push. He told two of the guys himself that he'd been out of line, and let Varun decide when, or whether, to come back. That night Varun nodded at him in the corridor. It wasn't much. Nitin didn't ask for more.

qa.q: What did Nitin blurt out at the terrace party?
qa.a: That Varun still wrote letters to his ex that he never sent.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel on Sunday morning?
qa.a: Sick with guilt and ashamed of betraying Varun's trust for a laugh.
He named exactly what he did and why, gave no excuse, owned it in front of others too, and accepted Varun's distance without pushing.

qa.q: How does Varun respond over the week?
qa.a: He stays hurt and distant at the other end of the table, offering only a small nod by Friday.

grounding: Shows sharing a friend's confidence for attention, then owning it quickly, apologising without excuses and accepting their distance.

passage:
Nandini, you asked why I'm so careful with other people's secrets. I'm Shalini aunty to you now, but at twenty-one I was just a hostel girl who liked being interesting.
My friend Leena told me she had failed one paper and was hiding it from her parents. One night, bored, I told it to three girls in the common room. For attention, nothing else.
When Leena found out, she asked me why. And I said the stupidest thing: "It's not a big deal, everyone fails a paper. You're overreacting." I made it her problem.
She moved rooms the next month. Years later I wrote her a proper apology, no excuses. She replied kindly. But the friendship never came back, and I understand why.
If you ever do what I did, own it the same day. Say sorry without a "but". And then let the other person decide how close to stand.

qa.q: What secret did Leena tell Shalini?
qa.a: That she had failed one paper and was hiding it from her parents.

qa.q: Why did Shalini tell the secret in the common room?
qa.a: She was bored and wanted attention; feeling interesting mattered more to her in that moment than Leena's trust.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Shalini's story, and what should she have done then?
qa.a: When Leena asked why; instead of calling it "not a big deal", Shalini should have owned it and apologised without excuses right away.

qa.q: How did Leena experience Shalini's response?
qa.a: As a second hurt: being told she was overreacting after her secret was spread, which is why she moved rooms.

grounding: Illustrates betraying a friend's confidence for attention and the harm of minimising it, with the lesson to own it and apologise without excuses.
